Hello Kwame Asante! I'm glad you reached out for advice. It's understandable that you're concerned about your friends' situation, especially with the community gathering coming up. While it's natural to want to help your friends resolve their issues, it's essential to consider whether it's truly your responsibility to "fix" the situation. Here are some points to ponder: 1. **You can't force reconciliation**: Ultimately, it's up to your friends to work through their differences and decide whether they want to repair their relationship. You can't force them to talk or reconcile if they're not ready. 2. **Respect their boundaries**: If your friends have decided to avoid each other, it's crucial to respect their boundaries and not push them to interact if they're not comfortable doing so. 3. **Your role is to support, not mediate**: As a friend, you can offer emotional support and a listening ear to both parties, but it's not your job to mediate their conflict or try to "fix" the situation. 4. **Focus on the community gathering**: Instead of trying to resolve the conflict, you could focus on finding ways to make the community gathering successful and enjoyable for everyone involved, regardless of your friends' relationship status. That being said, if you feel that your friends' conflict is affecting the community or the gathering, you could consider having an open and honest conversation with both of them separately. You might express your concerns and encourage them to find a way to coexist peacefully, at least for the sake of the community event. Remember, Kwame, your primary responsibility is to be a good friend and support your friends individually. AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I would say: 1 You are the asshole in this situation. While your intentions might have been good, you made a post about your friend without his consent, which is a violation of his privacy and boundaries. Your friend explicitly stated that he didn't want attention for his volunteer work and that he did it for self-improvement, not to seek praise or recognition. By making the post, you not only disregarded his wishes but also potentially made him feel uncomfortable, embarrassed, or even ashamed. Your friend's feelings and boundaries should have been respected, especially since you knew he wouldn't be able to see the post or respond to it for a week. It's not about whether the post was positive or negative; it's about respecting your friend's autonomy and decision to keep his volunteer work private. Your friend's shyness and quiet nature don't give you the right to speak on his behalf or share his personal experiences without his consent. It's essential to prioritize your friend's feelings and boundaries over your desire to praise or recognize him. In the future, it's crucial to ask for permission before sharing personal information or experiences about someone, especially if you know they might be sensitive about it.
